events.arc: The Back Half of the Lion
events.text: Lunar New Year, and the street's lion dance is one dancer short. The lion's head is spoken for by a big lad from the tannery. The back half, the part that is mostly bending over in the dark, is offered to you.

choices.text: Take the back half

effects.log: You spend the whole parade bent double, holding a stranger's belt and seeing only feet. When the lion bows to the magistrate's gate, you bow too, a beat late. The crowd roars. Your back aches for three days.

choices.text: Ask for the head instead

effects.log: The tannery lad laughs and lets you try it on. The head weighs more than you do. You topple into a stall of oranges, and the stall-keeper gives you one for the show.

events.arc: The Back Half of the Lion
events.text: Another New Year, another lion. You know the back half's secrets now: when to lift, when to wiggle, how to make the tail look like it has opinions. This year the front half is a newcomer who has never danced.

choices.text: Steer the newcomer from behind

effects.log: You hiss directions into the newcomer's spine the whole way: left, step, now shake. The lion has never looked so alive. Nobody but the two of you knows who was dancing it.

choices.text: Make the tail steal the show

effects.log: The tail wags at children, sulks at the butcher and sneezes at the magistrate. People talk about the lion with the clever bottom for a month.

events.arc: The Back Half of the Lion
events.text: The old lion costume is finally falling apart, and the street elders decide it is your turn to lead the dance. The head sits on your shoulders, heavy and painted, its eyes blinking on their strings.

choices.text: Dance it the old way, firecrackers and all

effects.log: You leap for the lettuce hung over the tea house door and get it on the second try. The whole street eats lettuce soup for luck.

choices.text: Teach two small children to be the back half

effects.log: They are terrible and they are wonderful. The lion staggers, sits down in the middle of the road and gets up again to cheers.

choices.text: Pay to have the old costume mended (15 taels)

effects.log: The tailor works through the night on the old lion's mane. It looks exactly as it did when you were small and bent double in the dark.

events.text: New Year visits. {npc} hands out red envelopes like everyone else, except that {his} have a riddle written on the front and the money is only yours if you solve it. The cousins groan. You look at yours.

choices.text: Solve it on the spot

effects.log: A thing with a mouth that never eats: a river. {npc} pays up with an enormous show of grief, and winks.

choices.text: Take it home and think

mem.note: ran to me with the answer

effects.log: You puzzle over it for three days and get it at dinner, mid-mouthful. You run all the way to {npc}'s door to say the answer. {He} pays double for the running.

events.text: {npc}'s riddles have got harder every year. This year's envelope holds no riddle at all, only a blank sheet and a note: Write me one I cannot solve.

choices.text: Write a fiendish riddle

effects.log: {npc} stares at it for the whole visit, then for a week. The answer comes back on a slip of paper with a coin and one word: Unfair.

choices.text: Write a riddle about {npc}

effects.log: A thing that gives away money it pretends to guard. {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down, and pins your riddle above the door.

events.text: Years of riddles. This New Year {npc} is slower, and hands the stack of red envelopes to you. 'Your turn. The little ones expect a riddle. Do not make them too easy.'

choices.text: Write riddles for every child in the house

effects.log: You are up past midnight inventing riddles about rivers, kettles and noses. The children groan exactly as you did. {npc} watches, very pleased.

choices.text: Fill them with easy riddles and extra coins (10 taels)

effects.log: Every child solves theirs and runs off rich. {npc} shakes {his} head at you. 'Soft,' {he} says, and steals one for later.

events.text: The firecrackers start at midnight, and the neighbour's yellow dog bolts down the lane in terror and squeezes under your bed. It is shaking so hard the bed rattles.

choices.text: Lie on the floor and talk to it until dawn

effects.log: You tell it everything you know, which is not much. By the last firecracker it is asleep with its head on your foot.

choices.text: Stuff cotton in its ears

effects.log: It looks at you with deep betrayal, then relief. It sleeps through the rest of the night like a sack of rice.

events.text: New Year again, and at the first bang the yellow dog is at your door before the smoke clears. It remembers. It scratches once, politely, and waits.

choices.text: Let it in, and make it a bed of old coats

effects.log: It circles three times and sighs the way old men sigh. Every New Year from then on, the coats are ready before midnight.

choices.text: Take it far up the hill, away from the noise

effects.log: You sit on the hill together and watch the town light up in little bursts below. From up here, the firecrackers look like flowers. The dog thinks so too.

events.text: The yellow dog has grown grey in the muzzle. This New Year it does not come running at the first bang. You find it lying by its own gate, too stiff to run, trembling.

choices.text: Carry it to your coats

effects.log: It weighs almost nothing now. It sleeps with its nose in your sleeve, and in the morning the neighbour finds you both and quietly brings a bowl of meat broth for each.

choices.text: Sit with it at its own gate till the noise ends

effects.log: You stay in the cold until the last firecracker. It is the dog's gate, after all. When the smoke clears, it thumps its tail once against your knee.

events.text: Before New Year every door in the lane needs its red couplets, and the old scholar who wrote them for forty years has gone to live with a daughter in the capital. The neighbours look at each other, then at you, because you once won a prize for neat characters.

choices.text: Grind the ink and write them all

effects.log: Thirty doors, sixty lines of good wishes. Your hand cramps by the twelfth door. By the thirtieth your characters look almost dignified.

choices.text: Write only your own, very carefully

effects.log: Yours are beautiful. The neighbours buy theirs at the market, and they are crooked. Everyone admires yours. Next year, they say, next year.

events.text: Your couplets are a tradition now. This year the baker wants one that mentions buns, the widow at the end wants one about her late husband's goat, and two brothers who are not speaking want one that says so politely.

choices.text: Write each one to order

effects.log: Buns of plenty, peace for the goat, and for the brothers: Two doors, one wall, one New Year. They read it, look at each other, and have dinner together for the first time in years.

choices.text: Write everyone the same lucky lines

effects.log: Prosperity and peace, thirty times over. Nobody complains, but the baker draws a small bun in the corner of his own.

events.text: A magistrate's clerk knocks: the magistrate has seen the couplets on your lane and wants a pair for the yamen gate. There will be a fee, and every official in the county will read them.

choices.text: Write a pair about honest government

effects.log: The magistrate reads them twice and pays you anyway. They hang there for a year, and a few people swear the clerks are a little politer.

choices.text: Write him something flattering

effects.log: The magistrate is delighted and pays handsomely. Your own lane's couplets that year are the best you have ever written, out of embarrassment.

choices.text: Say you only write for the lane

effects.log: The clerk goes away puzzled. Your lane is very proud of you, and the baker sends over a tray of buns.

events.text: Before New Year the paper Kitchen God by the stove goes up to heaven to report on the household, and you are told to smear honey on his lips so he only says sweet things. You have broken a bowl this year, and hidden it.

choices.text: Use a great deal of honey

effects.log: You glue the Kitchen God's mouth shut with half a jar. The grown-ups find you sticky to the elbows and laugh so hard nobody asks about the bowl.

choices.text: Confess about the bowl to the Kitchen God

effects.log: You whisper it to the paper face. It seems to listen. The next day you confess to the grown-ups too, and are hardly scolded at all.

events.text: This year you have been good, mostly. But a small cousin has eaten the offering sweets meant for the Kitchen God and is staring at you with sticky, guilty eyes.

choices.text: Replace the sweets with your own

effects.log: You give up your New Year sweets so the Kitchen God goes to heaven with a full stomach. The cousin follows you around adoringly for the rest of the holiday.

choices.text: Tell the Kitchen God it was the cousin

effects.log: You report it solemnly to the paper face. The cousin howls. Then you both laugh, and the grown-ups have no idea what is going on.

events.text: Your own stove now, and your own Kitchen God, paper and slightly crooked. You stand there with the honey and think about what this year was really like.

choices.text: Honey, and an honest word

effects.log: You tell the paper god the year as it was, good and bad. Then a little honey, for manners. The house feels lighter for it.

choices.text: Honey, and a very long list of requests

effects.log: Rain on time, fat chickens, a new roof, no more mice. The Kitchen God goes up in smoke with your list. That spring the mice leave. Possibly the cat did it.

events.text: New Year's Eve and the reunion dinner, and you are three days' walk from home in the snow. A letter from your mother, {npc}, says the same thing it always says: one empty seat is enough to make a whole table cold.

choices.text: Walk home through the snow

mem.note: walked home in the snow for the dinner

effects.log: You walk all night and arrive with frost in your eyebrows just as the dumplings come out. Your mother says nothing at all and gives you the biggest bowl.

choices.text: Send a letter and silver home instead (10 taels)

effects.log: The letter arrives on New Year's Day. Your mother writes back that the silver bought a fish and the fish was very fine, but it was not you.

events.text: This year you are home early. {npc} sets you to work: chopping, folding, carrying, and listening to every piece of news from every neighbour for the last ten years.

choices.text: Fold dumplings and listen to all of it

effects.log: By midnight you know who married whom, whose pig escaped and why the well tastes of iron. {npc} has not stopped smiling.

choices.text: Cook a dish of your own from the road

mem.note: cooked me a dish from the road

effects.log: You make a spiced dish you learned far away. {npc} eats it suspiciously, then asks for the recipe and says it needs more salt.

events.text: {npc}'s hands are too stiff to fold dumplings now. {He} sits at the head of the table and gives orders, and the youngest of the house are waiting to be shown how.

choices.text: Teach them the old way, pleat by pleat

mem.note: taught the little ones my dumplings

effects.log: Eighteen pleats, {npc} always said. The children manage nine. {npc} inspects every dumpling and approves them all.

choices.text: Let {npc} teach them, and be the hands

mem.note: was my hands at the reunion dinner

effects.log: {npc} talks, you fold. It is like being small again, except now you are the one doing it right.

events.text: At the New Year temple fair an old vendor with a copper pan blows hot sugar into figures: monkeys, dragons, roosters. {npc} sees you staring and asks which animal you are.

choices.text: Ask for a dragon

effects.log: {npc} puffs into a reed and the sugar swells into a dragon with whiskers. You do not eat it for a week. Then you do, all at once.

choices.text: Ask for a figure of yourself

mem.note: asked me for a sugar likeness

effects.log: {npc} squints at you and blows a little figure with your exact frown. You keep it on a shelf until the ants find it.

choices.text: Ask how it is done

effects.log: {npc} lets you blow into the reed. You make something with three legs and no head. {npc} says it is a perfect sugar ghost.

events.text: The temple fair again, and {npc}'s copper pan is in the same spot. {He} remembers you, and blows a sugar figure of you a year older without being asked. Today, though, a gang of boys has knocked over the sugar pan.

choices.text: Help clean up and stand guard

mem.note: stood guard over my sugar pan

effects.log: You scrape up what can be saved and glare at the gang until they leave. {npc} blows you a sugar general with a stern face.

choices.text: Buy the spoiled sugar so the day is not lost (5 taels)

effects.log: You buy a bag of broken sugar animals. {npc} adds a whole dragon for free, and you share the pieces with every child at the fair.

events.text: Years later, the temple fair. A young apprentice stands at {npc}'s copper pan, and {npc} sits beside it in a chair, wrapped in a quilt, directing. {He} sees you and taps the reed.

choices.text: Ask the apprentice for a figure of {npc}

mem.note: had a sugar figure made of me

effects.log: The apprentice blows a little old sugar vendor in a quilt. {npc} laughs until {he} coughs, and keeps it on the pan's edge all day.

choices.text: Let {npc} teach you one figure, properly

mem.note: learned the sugar rooster from me

effects.log: It takes all afternoon. Your rooster is lopsided but definitely a rooster. {npc} says that is how {he} started, sixty years ago.

events.text: The Lantern Festival, and riddles hang from every lantern. At the end of the bridge {npc} keeps a stall with the hardest riddles in the county: solve three and you win a lantern shaped like a carp. Nobody has won one for years. {npc} looks bored, and hopeful.

choices.text: Try the three riddles

ok.log: The moon in a well, a candle's shadow, a word with no beginning. You get all three. {npc} hands over the carp lantern as if it were a daughter's dowry, then shakes your hand for a long time.

fail.log: Two out of three. {npc} tells you the answer to the third, and you groan so loudly the people on the bridge turn round. 'Next year,' {he} says, delighted.

choices.text: Watch the others fail first

effects.log: You stand there all evening learning {npc}'s tricks. Every riddle has a pun hidden in it, and the pun is always cruel. You will be ready next year.

events.text: {npc}'s stall again. This year the riddles are new, and there is a fourth one pinned higher than the rest, written in {his} own hand. 'For you,' {he} says. 'I have been working on it all year.'

choices.text: Take on the fourth riddle

ok.log: It takes you until the lanterns are guttering, but you get it: it was {npc}'s own name, hidden in a poem. {He} laughs and gives you the brush to write next year's.

mem.note: is still thinking about my riddle

fail.log: You do not get it. {npc} will not tell you the answer. You spend the next year thinking about it at odd moments, which is exactly what {he} wanted.

choices.text: Write a riddle back for {npc}

mem.note: gave me a riddle at my own stall

effects.log: You pin yours beside {his}. {npc} reads it, frowns, reads it again, and closes the stall early to go home and think.

events.text: The bridge, the lanterns, the stall. {npc}'s hands shake as {he} pins the riddles up this year, and {he} asks you to hold the ladder. 'One day this stall will need a new keeper,' {he} says, not looking at you.

choices.text: Promise to keep the stall one day

effects.log: {npc} nods and pins up the last riddle without another word. Before the night is out {he} has taught you where the stall's planks are kept and which lantern hook is loose.

choices.text: Help {him} write riddles for the children

effects.log: Easy ones, for once. The children solve them in a rush and run off with paper lanterns. {npc} pretends to be annoyed and is not.

events.text: In the crush of the Lantern Festival crowd a small child is standing very still under a rabbit lantern, not crying, which is worse. {npc} has lost the grown-ups and is waiting, as told, under the rabbit.

choices.text: Lift {him} onto your shoulders to look

mem.note: carried me on their shoulders to find my aunt

effects.log: From up there {npc} spots a frantic aunt by the dumpling stall in no time. The aunt bows to you nine times and presses a rice cake on you.

choices.text: Buy {him} a sweet and wait under the rabbit

mem.note: waited with me under the rabbit lantern

effects.log: You wait together, sharing the sweet. After an hour the grown-ups find you, exactly where {npc} had promised to be.

events.text: Lantern night. A child pushes through the crowd and stops in front of you, holding a lopsided paper rabbit. It is {npc}, a year older. 'I made it,' {he} says. 'For if you get lost.'

choices.text: Accept the rabbit lantern gravely

effects.log: You hang it from your door. It falls apart in the spring rain, and you keep the bamboo frame.

choices.text: Make one together for next year

effects.log: You sit on the temple steps folding paper with {npc} until the candles burn low. The rabbit you make has the ears of a donkey.

events.text: Many lantern nights later, a grown stranger stops you on the bridge. It takes you a moment: it is {npc}, with a child of {his} own perched on {his} shoulders. 'I tell everyone this is how it is done,' {he} says.

choices.text: Buy the child a sweet, for old times

mem.note: bought my child a sweet under the lanterns

effects.log: The child takes it with the same solemn face {npc} once had. You all stand under the rabbit lantern for a while, not lost at all.

choices.text: Walk the festival together

mem.note: walked the lanterns with me again

effects.log: {npc} remembers every stall from that night, wrongly. You correct none of it. It is a much better story the way {he} tells it.

events.text: Every child carries a paper lantern on Lantern night, and you have made your own: a rabbit, with a candle inside. Ten steps from home the rabbit's ears catch fire.

choices.text: Run to the canal

effects.log: You plunge the rabbit into the canal. It is now a wet, smoking rabbit. Other children follow you for the rest of the night, impressed.

choices.text: Blow it out and keep walking

effects.log: You walk the whole festival with a rabbit that has no ears. Somebody's grandmother says it is the most honest lantern she has ever seen.

events.text: This year you have studied the problem. The candle sits on a little clay dish, the paper is waxed, and the rabbit has a chimney in its head. It looks very strange.

choices.text: Light it and hope

effects.log: It does not burn. It glows. Three children ask you to build theirs next year.

choices.text: Build three more for the neighbours' children

effects.log: You spend the week folding and waxing. On the night four chimneyed rabbits go down the lane together, and none of them catch fire.

events.text: Word has gone round. The lantern night before, there is a queue of children at your door with sheets of paper and very high hopes.

choices.text: Run a lantern workshop on your step

effects.log: Fish, rabbits, a dragon with a chimney, one thing nobody can name. The lane is the brightest in town, and nothing burns down.

choices.text: Teach the oldest children, and let them teach the rest

effects.log: By midnight the oldest are bossing the youngest about wax and chimneys. You sit back and drink tea, a master of lanterns.

events.text: Under the lanterns by the river someone has written a riddle on a lantern and left the answer blank. You write the answer. A voice behind you says, 'That was my riddle.' It is {npc}, looking at your handwriting.

choices.text: Ask {him} to write another

effects.log: {npc} writes one about the moon. You answer it. {He} writes another. By the time the lanterns go out, you have filled a whole lantern with riddles and answers.

choices.text: Apologise and offer to buy a new lantern (2 taels)

mem.note: bought me sweet soup by the river

effects.log: {npc} laughs and says the old one has your answer on it now and is worth more. You buy two sweet soups instead and talk until midnight.

events.text: Lantern night again. By the same river, on the same branch, hangs a lantern with a riddle written in {npc}'s hand. The answer, when you work it out, is your name.

choices.text: Write your answer, and a riddle of your own

mem.note: answered the riddle that was their name

effects.log: You write a riddle whose answer is {npc}'s name and hang it beside the first. Before the night is out the two of you are standing under both, not saying very much.

choices.text: Go and find {npc} in the crowd

mem.note: came to find me on lantern night

effects.log: It takes an hour. {npc} is by the sweet soup stall, pretending not to be waiting. 'It took you long enough,' {he} says.

events.text: The third lantern night. {npc} hands you a lantern with nothing written on it at all, and a brush. 'This one is yours to write,' {he} says. Half the street is pretending not to watch.

choices.text: Write a promise on it

mem.note: wrote me a promise on a lantern

effects.log: You write one line. {npc} reads it under the glow, and the lantern floats away down the river between you, burning steadily. Neither of you says anything for a long while.

choices.text: Write the worst riddle ever made

mem.note: made me laugh on lantern night

effects.log: {npc} reads it and laughs so hard the lantern shakes. 'Yes,' {he} says, which is not the answer to the riddle, but it will do.

events.text: The tea house holds a sweet rice dumpling eating contest every Lantern night. The champion, three years running, is {npc}, a porter with an iron stomach and no shame. {He} looks at you and taps the empty bowl.

choices.text: Eat for glory

mem.note: nearly beat me at the dumpling contest

ok.log: Thirty-one dumplings. {npc} eats thirty-two, then shakes your hand with a sticky hand. 'You will be dangerous next year,' {he} says.

fail.log: You stop at fourteen and lie down on the bench. {npc} eats forty, then eats your fifteenth out of kindness.

choices.text: Cheer for the underdog instead

effects.log: You cheer for a thin scholar who eats nine and faints happily. {npc} wins again and buys the scholar a bowl of ginger soup.

events.text: The contest again. {npc} is the champion, but {he} is limping: a crate fell on {his} foot at the docks. Everyone says this is your year.

choices.text: Eat your best and beat {him} fairly

mem.note: beat me fairly at the dumplings

effects.log: You win by two dumplings and nearly die of it. {npc} lifts your arm in triumph and announces that {he} will be back.

choices.text: Slow down and let {npc} win

effects.log: You stop at twenty with great theatre. {npc} sees exactly what you did, wins, and pays for your dinner afterwards without a word.

events.text: Years of dumpling contests. Now {npc} sits in the judge's chair with a belly that has finally retired, and a new young champion is boasting. {npc} catches your eye and nods at the empty bowl.

choices.text: Come out of retirement for {npc}

mem.note: came out of retirement for me

ok.log: You eat like a legend. The young champion goes pale at twenty-five. {npc} declares you champion and weeps a little, possibly from laughing.

fail.log: The young champion eats you into the ground. {npc} declares it an honourable defeat and the best show in years.

choices.text: Judge beside {npc}

effects.log: You two become the terror of the contest, arguing over every half-eaten dumpling. The crowd loves it more than the eating.

events.text: On Lantern night you write a wish on a sky lantern and let it go. It rises, wobbles, and comes down three streets away on somebody's roof.

choices.text: Go and fetch it

effects.log: The roof belongs to a widowed rope-maker who has already read your wish. 'It is a good wish,' the rope-maker says. 'I will send it up again for you next year.'

choices.text: Write another and try again

effects.log: The second goes up straight and high, until it is just another star. You never find out where the first one went.

events.text: A sky lantern drifts down into your yard on Lantern night. Your own old wish is on it, and under it, in a different hand: I hope this comes true. Your neighbour three streets away, the rope-maker.

choices.text: Write a wish for the rope-maker on it and send it up

effects.log: You add a line of your own and let it go. It rises properly this time. Somewhere three streets away, a door opens and someone watches it.

choices.text: Take the lantern back in person, with a pot of tea

effects.log: The rope-maker is very old and very glad of company. You drink tea on the roof where the lantern first came down, and watch the others go up.

events.text: Lantern night, and no lantern comes down. The rope-maker's house is shuttered; a nephew has taken the old one away to live by the sea. On your step, though, there is a coil of fine new rope and a folded sky lantern.

choices.text: Send the lantern up with both your wishes

effects.log: You write the rope-maker's wish from memory, and yours under it. It rises east, toward the sea, and does not come down.

choices.text: Keep the rope and the lantern

effects.log: You keep the rope by the door for years. It turns out to be the best rope you have ever owned, which is exactly the kind of gift the rope-maker would give.

events.arc: Pole Nine of the Dragon Lantern
events.text: The long dragon lantern needs eighteen carriers, and this year you are one of them: pole nine, the middle of the body, where the dragon bends.

choices.text: Follow the pole in front exactly

effects.log: You keep the dragon smooth through every turn. Nobody notices pole nine, which is the highest praise pole nine can get.

choices.text: Add a little wiggle of your own

effects.log: Pole nine shimmies. Poles eight and ten shimmy in panic. The dragon looks briefly alive and briefly seasick. The children love it.

events.arc: Pole Nine of the Dragon Lantern
events.text: The dragon lantern's paper skin is torn from last year's storm, and the old couple who mended it every year are too frail now. The street looks at the carriers.

choices.text: Spend the month mending the dragon

effects.log: Bamboo, paste and red paper. The old couple sit and supervise from their doorway. The dragon that comes out of your shed has a slightly surprised face, which suits it.

choices.text: Raise money for a new head (20 taels)

effects.log: You give the most and shame the rest into giving. The new head has bulging eyes and a pearl in its mouth. The old couple pronounce it nearly as good as theirs.

events.arc: Pole Nine of the Dragon Lantern
events.text: This year the street elders hand you the pearl: you are to run ahead of the dragon with the pearl on its pole and lead the whole beast through the town.

choices.text: Lead the dragon through every street

ok.log: You dart and feint and the dragon chases you through the whole town without a single tangle. People talk of it until summer.

fail.log: You turn too sharply at the fish market and the dragon ties itself in a knot around a lamp post. The crowd cheers louder than if it had gone right.

choices.text: Hand the pearl to the child who carried pole eighteen

effects.log: The child runs like the wind and the dragon follows, wobbling. You take pole nine again, where you belong.

events.text: Qingming is for sweeping graves and for flying kites, and the old saying goes that if you cut your kite loose, your bad luck flies away with it. Your kite is a swallow, and it is pulling hard.

choices.text: Cut it loose

effects.log: The swallow sails over the hills and out of sight. You feel very light, and slightly robbed.

choices.text: Hold on and bring it home

effects.log: You keep your kite and your bad luck both. The swallow hangs on your wall all year, looking smug.

events.text: A Qingming, a letter. A farmer from two valleys over writes that a swallow kite came down in the barley years ago, and that the children there have flown it every spring since. They would like to know whose it was.

choices.text: Write back and tell the kite's story

effects.log: A letter returns with a crayon drawing of the swallow, many times mended, and a dozen children holding the string. Your bad luck, it seems, became theirs and turned good.

choices.text: Make a new kite and send it to them (3 taels)

effects.log: You build a kite shaped like a carp and pay a carter to take it. The next spring two kites fly over the barley.

events.text: Qingming on the hill. A kite comes over the far ridge, battered and patched in a dozen colours. It is a swallow. Its string runs down to a gang of children who have walked two valleys to show you.

choices.text: Fly it with them

effects.log: It still pulls like it did when you were small. The children cheer. For a moment you are the same height as all of them.

choices.text: Teach them how to fix the spine

effects.log: You show them how to splint a kite's bamboo spine with thread. They go home with a swallow that will last another ten years.

events.text: Sweeping the graves at Qingming, you notice the grave beside yours is choked with weeds. Nobody has tended it for years. The name on the stone is half worn away.

choices.text: Sweep it too

effects.log: It takes an hour. Under the weeds the stone says: a ferry pilot, who carried people across the river for fifty years. You leave a cup of tea there.

choices.text: Ask the grave-keeper about it

effects.log: The grave-keeper says the pilot's family moved south a generation ago. 'Somebody should sweep it,' the grave-keeper adds, looking at your broom.

events.text: Qingming again, and you sweep both graves out of habit now. Someone is already standing at the pilot's stone: {npc}, dusty from a long road, holding a letter with a crude map.

choices.text: Tell {npc} who has been sweeping it

mem.note: swept my ancestor's grave for years

effects.log: {npc} stares at you, then bows very low. {He} came from the south to find a great-grandparent's grave and expected to find nothing but weeds.

choices.text: Help {npc} with the offerings

effects.log: You show {npc} how the rites are done here. {He} burns paper money for an ancestor {he} never met, and weeps a little, and laughs at the weeping.

events.text: Every Qingming since, {npc} has made the long journey north, and the two of you sweep both graves side by side and eat a cold lunch on the hill. This year {npc} brings a stonecutter.

choices.text: Have the pilot's name cut fresh

effects.log: The stonecutter cuts it deep: ferry pilot, fifty years on the river. {npc} insists your name goes on the back as the one who remembered.

choices.text: Have both graves' stones mended

mem.note: swept the graves with me every year

effects.log: Two stones, cut clean. {npc} pays for one and you pay for nothing at all, because {he} will not hear of it.

events.text: At Qingming children wear crowns of willow twigs, because the old ones say it keeps you from coming back as a yellow dog. A small neighbour's crown is too big and keeps falling over the child's eyes.

choices.text: Weave a smaller one for the little one

effects.log: It takes three tries. The small neighbour wears it all day and refuses to take it off at bedtime.

choices.text: Make yourself the biggest crown in the street

effects.log: Your crown is a whole willow bush. You can barely see. You are, however, safe from becoming a dog for at least a hundred lives.

events.text: The willow crown contest: the children of the street judge each other's crowns, and the prize is the honour of hanging willow over every door. A rival crown has birds' feathers in it.

choices.text: Add flowers to yours

effects.log: Willow, peach blossom and one stolen chrysanthemum. You win by a single vote, the small neighbour's.

choices.text: Vote for the feathered crown

effects.log: Feathers are hard to argue with. The rival child is so surprised that you are best friends by evening.

events.text: Years on, a small child at Qingming hands you a willow crown, badly woven and enormous. It is your old small neighbour's child. 'So you do not come back as a dog,' the child says.

choices.text: Wear it all day, very seriously

effects.log: You sweep graves, talk to elders and buy noodles in a willow crown. Nobody laughs. Several grown-ups quietly put theirs on too.

choices.text: Weave the child a smaller one in return

effects.log: Three tries. It fits. The child wears it to bed.

events.text: The day before Qingming no fire may be lit, by an old custom, and everybody eats cold food. You are starving by noon. The baker's cold green rice cakes are gone, and you are left with yesterday's cold millet.

choices.text: Eat the cold millet bravely

effects.log: It is terrible. It is also, somehow, very satisfying to suffer for an old custom. You understand your ancestors a little better.

choices.text: Invent a cold dish

effects.log: Cold millet, pickled radish, sesame and a whole lot of hope. The neighbours try it and ask for more.

events.text: Cold Food Day again. You have improved your cold millet into something with a reputation, and the baker from the next street wants the recipe for selling.

choices.text: Give the recipe away

effects.log: By next year every street in town eats your cold millet on Cold Food Day, and calls it by the baker's name.

choices.text: Sell it for a fair price

effects.log: The baker pays well, and thanks you on every bag. You do not get famous, but you do get free buns for a year.

events.text: Cold Food Day, and an old woman in the street has fallen ill and the physician says she must have hot soup. But no fire may be lit, and her family is torn.

choices.text: Light a fire and make the soup

effects.log: You make the soup. The street mutters, then the oldest elder says the ancestors would rather have a living grandmother than a cold kitchen. She is on her feet by Qingming.

choices.text: Carry hot stones from the bathhouse to warm it

effects.log: No flame is lit on your street. The soup is warm enough and the custom is kept. Everybody is a little bit proud of you.

events.text: Qingming is also for walking out in the new green, and by the river a group of townsfolk have spread mats and are passing a cup down a little channel: whoever the cup stops in front of must make a poem. It stops in front of you.

choices.text: Make a poem on the spot

ok.log: Four lines about a frog who thinks the spring is for him. People laugh, and then go quiet, because the last line is actually rather sad. You are asked back next year.

fail.log: You make a poem that rhymes 'river' with 'river'. The cup moves on. A kindly scholar tells you it was very pure.

choices.text: Drink the forfeit tea instead

effects.log: The forfeit is a cup of the bitterest tea in the province. You drink it bravely, and are applauded for courage, if not for poetry.

events.text: The river picnic again. This year an official's son has joined, very fine in silk, and he is making a show of mocking everyone's poems.

choices.text: Answer him with a poem

ok.log: A poem about a peacock who tried to swim. The river bank howls. The official's son laughs too, finally, and brings better manners next year.

fail.log: Your poem is not good enough to be cutting, only rude. The picnic goes cool. You walk home with the frog poem playing in your head instead.

choices.text: Ignore him and praise everyone else's

effects.log: You praise the farmer's poem, the widow's, the child's. Soon he is the only one nobody is listening to, and he goes quiet on his own.

events.text: The river picnic has become a little society, and they want you to keep the cup this year: to decide where it starts, and to make the first poem.

choices.text: Start it with the child who never speaks

effects.log: The child whispers four lines about a heron. The whole bank goes very still. That child keeps the cup ten years later.

choices.text: Make a poem about all the springs before

effects.log: You name everyone who sat here once and does not now. People raise their cups to the water. It is the best afternoon of the year.

events.text: Qingming on the hill with {npc}, who knows every grave in the family: who was clever, who was a thief, who planted the pear tree. {He} makes you repeat the names back.

choices.text: Learn every name

mem.note: learned every name on the hill

effects.log: Great-grandfather the stubborn, great-aunt the singer, a cousin who fell out of the pear tree and laughed. You say them all. {npc} gives you a boiled egg, which is the highest honour.

choices.text: Ask for the stories instead

mem.note: wanted the stories of the dead

effects.log: {npc} tells you about the thief in such detail that you suspect {he} was there. The names come later, with the stories stuck to them.

events.text: The hill again. {npc} stops halfway up and has to sit on a stone. 'Go on,' {he} says. 'You know them. Sweep them and come and tell me who you found.'

choices.text: Sweep them all and come back with every name

mem.note: swept the family graves for me

effects.log: You come back down and recite them in order. {npc} corrects one name, and you are not sure {he} is right, and you let {him} be.

choices.text: Carry {npc} up the rest of the way

effects.log: {npc} protests all the way to the top. At the top {he} stops protesting and sits among the stones, naming each one with a hand on it.

events.text: Qingming, and you climb the hill with the younger ones of the house. {npc} has stayed home this year with a blanket and a pot of tea, and made you promise to teach them properly.

choices.text: Teach them the names, and the stories

mem.note: taught the little ones the names

effects.log: Great-grandfather the stubborn, great-aunt the singer. The youngest asks who {npc} will be, one day. You say: the one who remembered all of them.

choices.text: Bring the children home to tell {npc} what they found

mem.note: brought the children home to me

effects.log: They tumble in shouting names, half of them wrong. {npc} laughs and corrects every one, which is what {he} wanted.

events.text: Dragon Boat Festival, and the river town's boat is a rower short. The crew captain, a ferry hand with forearms like hams, hands you a paddle and points at the bench nearest the drum.

choices.text: Row your heart out

ok.log: Your paddle bites in time with the drum the whole length of the river. The town's boat comes second, which is its best result in nine years. The crew carries you to the noodle shop.

fail.log: You catch a crab with your paddle halfway down and nearly go in. The boat comes fifth. The captain says that every rower does it once, and buys you noodles anyway.

choices.text: Ask to beat the drum instead

effects.log: The drummer is a nine-year-old with no rhythm, who is grateful to be replaced. You find the beat in the second stretch, and the boat flies.

events.text: The race again. The town upstream has a new boat with a carved head that is, everyone agrees, a little too big. Their crew has been calling your town's boat the Leaky Eel for weeks.

choices.text: Race to beat the upstream boat

ok.log: You beat them by a dragon's length. The upstream crew are good losers in the end, and the two crews eat zongzi together on the bank until dark.

fail.log: They beat you by a whisker, and their drummer bows so low he falls out. Both crews laugh until it hurts.

choices.text: Paint a better face on the Leaky Eel first

effects.log: You stay up two nights painting fierce eyes and gold scales. The Leaky Eel loses the race but wins the crowd. Nobody calls it the Leaky Eel again.

events.text: This year the crew asks you to be captain. The old captain's shoulders have gone, and he sits on the bank with a drum of his own, beating time for nobody.

choices.text: Captain the boat

effects.log: You call the stroke from the prow. The boat does not win, but it does not catch a single crab all race. The old captain's drum on the bank keeps time with yours the whole way.

choices.text: Put the old captain in the prow with the drum

effects.log: He weeps a little, then beats the drum like a thunderstorm. The crew rows like they are twenty. Second place, and the loudest boat on the river.

events.text: Before Dragon Boat Festival the whole lane wraps zongzi, sticky rice in bamboo leaves, and {npc} next door wraps them faster than anyone alive. {He} watches you struggle with a leaf and clicks {his} tongue.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you

mem.note: learned to wrap zongzi from me

effects.log: Fold, cup, fill, fold, tie. Yours leak. {npc} shows you again, and again. By the end of the day you have made one zongzi that holds, and {npc} eats it to celebrate.

choices.text: Keep trying your own way

effects.log: Your zongzi are the shape of potatoes. {npc} eats one, chews thoughtfully, and says the inside is very good and the outside is a crime.

events.text: {npc}'s zongzi have a secret, and this year {he} says you are ready to know it. A salted egg yolk, a sliver of pork, and a strip of dried tangerine peel, put in last, which nobody else in the lane does.

choices.text: Wrap a hundred with {npc}

mem.note: wrapped a hundred zongzi with me

effects.log: You wrap until your fingers ache. The lane gets {npc}'s zongzi as usual, except half of them are yours, and nobody can tell.

choices.text: Suggest a secret of your own

effects.log: You add a few red beans. {npc} frowns, tastes, frowns harder, and then quietly starts adding red beans to {his} own.

events.text: {npc} cannot fold the leaves any more; the fingers will not close. On the festival morning {he} sits at your table while you wrap, and tastes the first one out of the pot.

choices.text: Wrap them all {npc}'s way

effects.log: Tangerine peel, last. {npc} eats it slowly and nods once, which from {npc} is a whole speech.

choices.text: Take the zongzi round the lane in {npc}'s name

mem.note: carried my zongzi round the lane

effects.log: You knock on every door: these are from {npc}. People come out to {npc}'s step all afternoon to say thank you.

events.text: On Dragon Boat day the grown-ups paint the character for king on the children's foreheads with yellow realgar paste, to keep away the five poisonous creatures. Yours is crooked and enormous.

choices.text: Wear it proudly all day

effects.log: You walk round the market like a small king. A stallholder gives you a plum because kings should have plums.

choices.text: Paint kings on the dog, the cat and the goat

effects.log: The goat objects. The cat leaves home for a day. The dog wears its king with dignity. The grown-ups are laughing too hard to scold you.

events.text: Dragon Boat day again. A toad, one of the five poisonous creatures, has hopped into the kitchen, and every grown-up in the house is out at the river.

choices.text: Show the toad your painted forehead

effects.log: The toad looks at the king on your forehead and leaves. You are completely certain the paste worked.

choices.text: Carry the toad outside in a bowl

effects.log: It is just a toad, and quite a polite one. You put it in the garden, where it eats the slugs all summer.

events.text: Dragon Boat morning, and the small ones of the street line up in front of you with foreheads ready: somehow you have become the person who paints the kings.

choices.text: Paint every king perfectly

effects.log: Thirty small kings, every stroke straight. They march to the river like an army. You never had a straight one yourself.

choices.text: Paint them crooked and enormous, the old way

effects.log: They look wonderful. A small one asks if it is meant to be crooked. You say yes, that is how the strongest kings are painted.

events.text: They say that at exactly noon on Dragon Boat day, an egg will stand on its end. The whole courtyard is crouched over eggs, waiting for the sun.

choices.text: Balance your egg at noon

ok.log: It stands. You hold your breath. It goes on standing. You do not touch it again until the evening.

fail.log: It rolls off the step and breaks. A neighbour's hen comes and eats it, which is also a kind of luck.

choices.text: Watch everyone else's eggs

effects.log: You learn that the eggs stand at any hour if your hands are patient enough, and say nothing, because noon is more fun.

events.text: The egg contest has become serious in your courtyard: whoever stands the most eggs at noon is champion for a year. A boy from the next yard has brought a basket of twenty.

choices.text: Stand as many as you can

ok.log: Eleven eggs, standing in a ring. The boy from the next yard stands twelve, and gives you his best egg as a prize for a fine ring.

fail.log: Your hands shake. Two eggs. The boy stands nineteen and is insufferable until autumn.

choices.text: Cook all the eggs into one great omelette for the yard

effects.log: Nobody stands any eggs. Everybody eats very well. You are not champion, but you are extremely popular.

events.text: At noon on Dragon Boat day, a child is crouched over an egg in your yard, scowling at it. It will not stand.

choices.text: Show the child the trick

effects.log: Patience, a grain of salt, a still breath. The egg stands. The child stares at you as if you were an immortal.

choices.text: Tell the child it only works at noon, and wait

effects.log: At the exact stroke of noon, the child's egg stands. The child is sure it was the sun. So, to be honest, are you.

events.text: In the chaos of the dragon boat race a spectator on a crowded jetty is shoved into the river and goes under, flailing. It is {npc}, a stranger in good clothes that are now pulling {him} down.

choices.text: Dive in after {him}

mem.note: pulled me out of the river

ok.log: You haul {npc} up by the collar and onto the jetty, coughing river. The crowd cheers you louder than the winning boat. {npc} grips your hand and cannot speak.

fail.log: You get {npc} out, but swallow half the river doing it. You lie on the jetty beside {him}, both of you coughing, while a dog licks your face.

choices.text: Throw a mooring rope

effects.log: The rope lands right across {npc}'s shoulders. You and three fishermen pull {him} in. {npc} bows to everyone dripping wet and then sneezes.

events.text: Dragon Boat day, a year later. {npc} finds you on the bank, dry this time, with a boy carrying a basket of the best zongzi in the county. 'A year of life,' {npc} says. 'I owe you at least this.'

choices.text: Share the zongzi with {npc} on the bank

effects.log: You watch the race together and argue about which boat is best. {npc} is a silk merchant, it turns out, and very bad at choosing boats.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to learn to swim instead

effects.log: {npc} laughs, then sees you are serious. That summer {he} takes lessons from a fisherman's child, and writes to you about every stroke.

events.text: This Dragon Boat day {npc} is not on the bank but in the river, in a boat, with a paddle. 'I can swim,' {he} shouts. 'I joined a crew. Watch!'

choices.text: Cheer {npc}'s boat home

effects.log: {npc}'s boat comes last by a long way, and {npc} is the happiest rower on the river. Afterwards {he} buys every crew a round of tea in your name.

choices.text: Jump in a boat and race {him}

effects.log: Your boat beats {npc}'s by a length. {npc} splashes you with a paddle on purpose. You both end up in the river, both swimming this time.

events.text: On Dragon Boat morning the children have threads of five colours tied round their wrists for health. The custom says you must not cut them until the first summer rain, and throw them in the stream.

choices.text: Wait for the first rain

effects.log: You guard the threads for weeks. When the rain comes you run out and throw them in the stream, and you are not ill once all summer.

choices.text: Give your threads to a sick child down the lane

effects.log: The child wears two sets of threads and recovers by midsummer. You are pretty sure that was the threads.

events.text: This year you twist the five threads yourself: blue, red, white, black and yellow, for the five directions. There is a lot of thread and a lot of wrists in the lane.

choices.text: Tie threads for every child in the lane

effects.log: You go door to door. By noon the whole lane has coloured wrists, and the old midwife says it has been years since anyone did it properly.

choices.text: Twist one very fine set to sell (4 taels)

effects.log: You buy good silk thread and twist a set as fine as a jeweller's. A merchant's wife buys it for her son and orders ten more.

events.text: Dragon Boat morning, and a very small child holds out a wrist to you and waits. It does not seem to matter that you are not kin.

choices.text: Tie the threads and tell the custom

effects.log: First summer rain, then into the stream. The child nods solemnly. Weeks later you see a small figure running out into the rain.

choices.text: Let the child tie threads on your wrist too

effects.log: The knot is terrible. You wear it until the first summer rain anyway, through a meeting with very serious people.

events.text: The two villages on the river have raced each other on Dragon Boat day for a hundred years, and fought after the race for about ninety of them. This year a quarrel about a fishing weir has made it worse.

choices.text: Row, and keep out of the fight

effects.log: You row hard, lose by a hair, and spend the fight afterwards holding the noodle seller's stall upright so it does not fall over.

choices.text: Go upstream and look at the weir

effects.log: The weir really does block half the river. The upstream elders say it was there first. Everyone is right, which is the worst kind of quarrel.

events.text: This year the race is cancelled for the quarrel. No boats, no drums, no zongzi on the bank. Both villages are miserable and too proud to say so.

choices.text: Suggest one boat with both crews in it

effects.log: It takes three weeks of talking. On Dragon Boat day one enormous boat goes down the river with both villages rowing and arguing. It wins, against nobody.

choices.text: Fix the weir so the river runs both ways

ok.log: You and some sulking volunteers from both sides move half the weir's stones in a week. The fish come through. The race is back the next year.

fail.log: The stones are heavier than the quarrel. You hurt your back and the weir stays. But both villages bring you soup, which is a start.

events.text: Dragon Boat day, and both villages' boats are on the river again, painted, proud, ready. The elders of both sides have asked you to start the race.

choices.text: Fire the starting cracker

effects.log: Bang. Two dragons leap off the line. Upstream wins by a nose. There is no fight afterwards, only zongzi, which is the first time in ninety years.

choices.text: Declare the winner before it starts: the river

effects.log: Both villages laugh at you, then at themselves. They race anyway, and the loser buys the winner's noodles, which becomes the new custom.

events.text: Qixi night, and in the courtyard the children float needles on a bowl of water in the moonlight. If the needle's shadow looks like a flower or a cloud, the Weaver Girl has given you skilful hands.

choices.text: Float your needle carefully

ok.log: The shadow at the bottom of the bowl looks like a plum blossom, more or less. You are told your hands will be clever. You decide to believe it.

fail.log: Your needle sinks like a stone. The shadow looks like a stone. The old aunts say that means very strong hands, which is also good.

choices.text: Float a whole handful of needles

effects.log: The bowl is a mess of shadows: a cloud, a fish, a broom, a rabbit with five legs. The old aunts cannot agree what it means and argue happily all night.

events.text: Qixi again, and the needle has become a contest: whoever's needle makes the finest shadow gets first pick of the melons. Your cousin has practised all year.

choices.text: Practise all afternoon beforehand

effects.log: Your needle floats like a leaf and its shadow is a perfect little cloud. First pick of the melons. Your cousin sulks until you share.

choices.text: Help your cousin float the best one

effects.log: The cousin's shadow is a lotus. The cousin gets the melon and gives you half, then the bigger half.

events.text: Qixi night. You have not floated a needle in years, but somebody has set out a bowl of water in the moonlight, and there is a needle beside it, waiting.

choices.text: Float it, for the child you were

effects.log: The shadow is a crooked little star. Your hands have done a lot since the last time, good and bad. You decide the Weaver Girl approves.

choices.text: Call the children of the house to float theirs

effects.log: You teach them the trick: a dry needle, a still bowl, a slow hand. Five shadows, five arguments. A very good Qixi.

events.text: Qixi, the night the Herdsman and the Weaver cross the bridge of magpies to meet. On the town's own little stone bridge, where the young go to watch the stars, {npc} is standing alone and looking up.

choices.text: Ask {npc} which stars are the lovers

mem.note: watched the Qixi stars with me

effects.log: {npc} points them out: the Weaver, the Herdsman, the river of stars between. Then {he} points out a dozen more, and makes half of them up, and admits it.

choices.text: Stand a little way off and watch the sky too

mem.note: stood on the bridge with me

effects.log: After an hour of silence {npc} says, without looking over, 'They only get one night.' You say that seems unfair. {He} laughs.

events.text: Qixi again. The little stone bridge, the stars. {npc} is there, and turns as you come up the steps as if {he} has been listening for your feet all year.

choices.text: Bring {npc} a pair of sweet Qixi pastries

mem.note: brought me Qixi pastries on the bridge

effects.log: You share them on the bridge and talk about the whole year, every small thing. The magpies, everyone agrees, did good work.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you came only for the stars

mem.note: pretended to come for the stars

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, and at the stars, and back. 'Liar,' {he} says, very fondly.

events.text: A third Qixi on the bridge. {npc} says {he} does not want to wait for one night a year, like the Herdsman and the Weaver. 'Some stories should be better than that.'

choices.text: Agree, and walk {npc} home

mem.note: said our story would be better

effects.log: You walk home the long way, by the river, and do not hurry. The stars are still there in the morning, which surprises nobody but you.

choices.text: Say you will come every Qixi, whatever else changes

effects.log: {npc} takes your hand and holds it a long time on the bridge. It is a promise, and both of you know it.

events.text: An old Qixi custom: catch a spider, keep it in a little box overnight, and in the morning the web it spins shows how skilful you will be. You have caught a fat garden spider and named it General.

choices.text: Give General a big box and a dead fly

effects.log: In the morning General has spun a web like a fishing net, broad and sturdy. The grown-ups say you will have strong, sure hands.

choices.text: Give General a tiny box

effects.log: General spins a tiny perfect web like lace. The grown-ups say fine, delicate work. You say General is a genius.

events.text: Qixi again. The children of the street compare spider boxes in the morning. A neighbour's child has a spider that has spun nothing at all and is crying about it.

choices.text: Say an empty box means a free spirit

effects.log: The child cheers up at once and tells everyone. By noon, half the street wishes their spider had spun nothing.

choices.text: Give the child General's web

effects.log: You carry it over on a twig. The child stops crying. General, back in the garden, spins another by evening.

events.text: Qixi night, and you find a box on the window sill with a note from a small hand: For General's grandchildren. There is a spider in it, and it has already started a web.

choices.text: Keep the spider overnight, the old way

effects.log: In the morning there is a web like a little wheel. You show it to the child who left the note, who says it means you will be clever. You say it is rather late for that.

choices.text: Let the spider go in the garden

effects.log: It walks off into the beans. The child is disappointed, then decides the beans are General's kingdom. Every Qixi after, you are both careful in the beans.

events.text: Qixi, and {npc} hands you a folded paper at supper without a word. Inside, one line: You still burn the rice, and I would not change it.

choices.text: Write one line back

mem.note: wrote me a line at Qixi

effects.log: You think all evening. Your line: You still snore, and I listen for it. {npc} reads it and laughs into {his} sleeve.

choices.text: Cook the rice perfectly, as an answer

effects.log: You stand over the pot for an hour. The rice is perfect. {npc} is almost disappointed, and eats three bowls.

events.text: Another Qixi, another folded line under your bowl. The box where you keep them is getting heavy. Tonight's says: Do you remember the first one?

choices.text: Read all the old lines aloud together

effects.log: Years of them. Rice, snoring, the time the roof leaked, the time you were both too stubborn to speak for a week. You laugh until the lamp goes out.

choices.text: Write the first line again, from memory

effects.log: You get it word for word. {npc} looks at you a long time and says you are a sentimental fool, and keeps that paper inside {his} sleeve.

events.text: Qixi again. {npc}'s hand shakes as {he} writes now, and tonight's line is only three words long. You read it twice.

choices.text: Write three words back

effects.log: Three words, the same three. You fold it and put it in {npc}'s sleeve. {npc} pretends not to notice, and smiles all evening.

choices.text: Take {npc} out to watch the stars

mem.note: watched the Qixi stars with me

effects.log: Two old lovers on a bench, looking for the Weaver and the Herdsman. You both point at the wrong stars and agree they are right.

events.text: On Qixi evening an old ox-herd sits by the village gate and tells the story of the Herdsman and the Weaver to anyone who stops. {npc} tells it differently from how you heard it. In {npc}'s version, the ox is the hero.

choices.text: Stop and listen to the ox's version

effects.log: The ox, says {npc}, saw everything and gave the Herdsman good advice. The ox was the clever one. You go home and look at oxen differently.

choices.text: Argue that the Weaver is the hero

mem.note: argued about the ox with me

effects.log: {npc} is delighted to have an argument. You debate until the stars come out and the real Herdsman and Weaver are overhead, ignoring you both.

events.text: {npc}'s Qixi story again, and the ox has grown more heroic. This year the ox also invented the plough, rescued a magpie and gave a speech to the Jade Emperor.

choices.text: Ask what happened to the ox in the end

effects.log: {npc} goes quiet. The ox, {he} says, grew old, and the Herdsman wore its hide to fly to heaven, so the ox went too. Then {he} blows {his} nose very loudly.

choices.text: Add a part where the ox wins a dragon boat race

mem.note: gave the ox a boat race

effects.log: {npc} takes it into the story at once and tells it for years afterwards. Children in the village believe it absolutely.

events.text: Qixi evening. {npc} is too hoarse to tell the story this year. The village children are sitting by the gate anyway, and {npc} looks at you.

choices.text: Tell the ox's version for {npc}

effects.log: You tell it the way {npc} does, with the plough and the speech and the boat race. {npc} mouths every word. The children cheer the ox.

choices.text: Get {npc} to whisper it and repeat it aloud

effects.log: {npc} whispers, you shout. It is the best telling the story has ever had. Even the real oxen in the field look over.

events.text: Qixi brings out the town matchmaker, {npc}, who has decided that you are the great unfinished work of {his} career. {He} arrives with a list of seven candidates and a portrait of each.

choices.text: Look at the portraits politely

effects.log: A butcher's heir, a widowed tea seller, a poet with a squint. You say kind things about all of them. {npc} writes down every kind thing as a sign of interest.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you will choose for yourself

effects.log: {npc} says everybody says that. {He} leaves the portraits on your table anyway, in case you change your mind in the night.

events.text: {npc} is back for Qixi with a longer list and a new tactic: a tea at {his} house, where all seven candidates will happen to be at once.

choices.text: Go, and be charming to all seven

effects.log: It is the most awkward afternoon of your life and also very funny. Three of the candidates end up matched with each other. {npc} counts it as a great success.

choices.text: Send {npc} a basket of pastries and a firm no

effects.log: {npc} eats the pastries and sends a note: Firm noes are my favourite. They are the ones who marry within the year.

events.text: Qixi. {npc} sits on your step without a list for once. 'I have matched four hundred couples,' {he} says, 'and the one person I cannot match is you. Tell me what you actually want.'

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth

mem.note: told me the truth at last

effects.log: You talk for an hour. {npc} listens, says nothing for once, and leaves with a thoughtful face. You have a feeling you will be seeing more of {his} lists.

choices.text: Set {npc} up with the widowed tea seller instead

effects.log: {npc} is outraged, then thoughtful, then seen at the tea stall three evenings running. By the next Qixi, the matchmaker is matched.

events.text: Before Mid-Autumn the old pear-wood mooncake mould comes down from the shelf. It is cracked straight through the rabbit in the middle, and the mooncakes come out with a rabbit that has a scar.

choices.text: Use it anyway

effects.log: Scarred rabbits all round. The neighbours call them warrior rabbits and ask for more.

choices.text: Try to carve a new mould

effects.log: You ruin two blocks of pear wood and your thumb. The third mould has a rabbit that looks like a surprised cat. You are very proud of it.

events.text: Mid-Autumn again, and you have practised carving all year. This mould could be your best: a rabbit, a moon, a cassia tree, and a border of clouds.

choices.text: Carve it to the last cloud

ok.log: The mooncakes come out crisp as a seal: rabbit, moon, tree, every cloud. An old baker from the market offers to buy the mould. You refuse, then lend it to him for a week.

fail.log: The clouds come out as blobs. The rabbit is perfect. People say the blobs are a very modern kind of cloud.

choices.text: Mend the old cracked mould instead

effects.log: You glue and pin the pear wood. The warrior rabbit is still scarred, just less. You realise you like it better than any new rabbit.

events.text: Mid-Autumn. A young neighbour asks to borrow your moulds, then asks to watch you carve, then asks to learn.

choices.text: Teach the young one to carve

effects.log: The first rabbit looks like a potato. The tenth looks like a rabbit. By next Mid-Autumn the young one's mould is better than yours, and you say so.

choices.text: Give the young one the old scarred mould

effects.log: The young one cannot believe it. That Mid-Autumn the whole lane eats warrior rabbits, and the old mould is back in use for another forty years.

events.text: Mid-Autumn night in the courtyard, and {npc} points up at the full moon. 'See the rabbit? It pounds the medicine of immortality all year, and never once has it eaten any.'

choices.text: Look for the rabbit until you see it

mem.note: found the moon rabbit with me

effects.log: You find it after a long time: ears, mortar, pestle. Once you have seen it you can never unsee it. {npc} is very satisfied.

choices.text: Ask why the rabbit never eats any

effects.log: {npc} thinks hard. 'Because it is waiting for someone,' {he} says, and will not say who. You think about it all year.

events.text: Mid-Autumn again, mooncakes and the moon. {npc} asks if you have worked out who the rabbit is waiting for.

choices.text: Say: for the moon lady, its friend

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. 'Not bad. Not right, but not bad.' {He} gives you the yolk from {his} mooncake as a prize.

choices.text: Say: for whoever needs the medicine most

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a long time. Then {he} hugs you so hard you drop your mooncake.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, and {npc} has grown frail. In the courtyard {he} cannot see the moon very well now, and asks you to tell {him} if the rabbit is still there.

choices.text: Describe the rabbit, pounding away

mem.note: saw the moon rabbit for me

effects.log: You tell {npc} every detail: the ears, the mortar, the cassia tree. {npc} smiles with {his} eyes shut. 'Still waiting,' {he} says.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the rabbit is finally eating the medicine

mem.note: made me laugh at the moon

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud, the first time in weeks. 'About time,' {he} says. You both eat an extra mooncake, for the rabbit.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, and you are far from home, in an inn whose roof leaks. The full moon comes over the hills, and somewhere far off your father, {npc}, is looking at it too.

choices.text: Write home by the moonlight

effects.log: The letter is mostly about the leaking roof. At the end you write that the moon is the same here. Months later, a reply: it is the same here too.

choices.text: Buy a mooncake and share it with the innkeeper (2 taels)

effects.log: The innkeeper is far from home too. You split the mooncake and both pretend the other one is family.

events.text: Mid-Autumn again, and a letter arrives in {npc}'s blocky hand just before the festival: Look at the moon at the hour of the rat. I will look too.

choices.text: Climb the highest roof at the hour of the rat

mem.note: looked at the moon with me from far away

effects.log: You sit on the ridge of the inn with the moon on your face. Far away {npc} is doing the same. It is the closest you have been all year.

choices.text: Write back with the exact time you looked

mem.note: kept the moon hour with me

effects.log: Your letter crosses {npc}'s on the road. Both say the same hour. {npc}'s also says the dog has been eating the plums.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, and you are home. {npc} is in the courtyard at the hour of the rat, looking up out of habit, and turns round and sees you.

choices.text: Look at the moon together, at last

effects.log: Neither of you says much. {npc} hands you a mooncake {he} has been saving. It is stale. It is the best mooncake you have ever eaten.

choices.text: Tell {npc} about every moon you saw away

effects.log: Moons over rivers, over deserts, over a burning city. {npc} listens and says, at the end, that none of them was as good as this one. You agree.

events.text: A stranger at the Mid-Autumn market buys two mooncakes, gives you one, and walks off. When you break it open there is a slip of paper inside. It says: The willow by the east well. Midnight.

choices.text: Go to the willow at midnight

effects.log: Nobody comes. On the willow's lowest branch hangs a little bag with a copper coin and a second slip: Not you. But thank you for coming.

choices.text: Hand the slip to the night watch

effects.log: The watchman reads it, laughs, and says it is a lovers' meeting place and you have spoiled somebody's evening. You feel terrible and buy him a cup of tea.

events.text: Mid-Autumn market, a year later. The same stranger buys two mooncakes and gives you one with a little bow. Inside: Last year I mixed up my mooncakes. This year it is for you. Thank you for going to the willow.

choices.text: Go and find the stranger

effects.log: The stranger is a shy old letter-writer who sends messages in mooncakes for people too shy to speak. Last year's lovers are married now. You are both very pleased about it.

choices.text: Send a message back in a mooncake

effects.log: You write: Who are you? The next morning a mooncake is left on your step. Inside: A friend of the willow. You never learn more, and decide not to try.

events.text: A young neighbour comes to you at Mid-Autumn, red to the ears, holding a mooncake and a slip of paper. The young one has heard you know how messages in mooncakes are done.

choices.text: Help the young one bake the message in

effects.log: You show how to hide a slip so it does not burn. On the festival night, the young one gives the mooncake away and runs. Next spring, there is a wedding.

choices.text: Say the willow by the east well is a better place

effects.log: The young one goes to the willow at midnight with the mooncake. You go too, very quietly, to make sure. Someone else is already waiting there.

events.text: At Mid-Autumn the town's poets hire a flat boat and drift under the full moon, drinking tea and making verses. {npc}, a poet with ink on {his} cuffs, waves you aboard.

choices.text: Make a verse about the moon

ok.log: Your verse: the moon has seen every face on this river and forgotten none. The boat goes quiet, then {npc} writes it down.

fail.log: Your verse rhymes moon with moon. {npc} says that takes courage, and pours you more tea.

choices.text: Just listen and row

effects.log: You row the poets round the bend. {npc} recites all night. When you land, {he} gives you a poem {he} wrote about the rower.

events.text: The moon boat again. This year {npc} is in a dark mood: a rival poet has published a collection that steals three of {npc}'s best lines.

choices.text: Write a poem mocking the thief

mem.note: mocked the thief who stole my lines

effects.log: Your poem is so funny it gets copied in every teahouse. The thief's book is remembered mostly for being in it.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to write better lines

effects.log: {npc} glares, then laughs, then writes all night. {His} next collection is the best thing {he} ever did.

events.text: The moon boat, years on. {npc} is old now, and has asked to be rowed out alone with you. {He} wants to make one more verse before the moon sets.

choices.text: Row slowly, and wait for it

effects.log: The verse comes at last, very short, about the river keeping everything. {npc} asks you to keep it. You know it by heart before you reach the shore.

choices.text: Make the verse together, line by line

mem.note: made a verse with me on the river

effects.log: One line each, back and forth, until the moon is down. Nobody else ever hears it. That is the point.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, and after the mooncakes are eaten {npc} pulls two stools into the yard so you can sit under the moon. The neighbours' children are shrieking somewhere. The tea is going cold.

choices.text: Sit and say nothing

mem.note: sat with me under the moon

effects.log: You sit for an hour without saying a word. It is the best conversation you have had all year.

choices.text: Point out the rabbit

mem.note: argued about the moon with me

effects.log: {npc} says it is clearly a toad. You argue until the moon has moved a hand's width. Nobody wins.

events.text: The stools come out at Mid-Autumn again. This year it is cloudy, and there is no moon at all.

choices.text: Sit out anyway and wait

mem.note: waited out the clouds with me

effects.log: Near midnight the clouds tear for a moment, and there it is. You both cheer like children.

choices.text: Draw a moon on paper and hang it up

effects.log: You hang a paper moon on the plum tree. {npc} laughs so hard the neighbours look over the wall. You sit under the paper moon all evening.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, the two stools, the moon. {npc}'s stool has a cushion on it now, and a blanket, and {npc} still insists on carrying the teapot out unaided.

choices.text: Let {npc} carry it

effects.log: It takes a long time, and none of it spills. You do not offer to help once. {npc} is enormously pleased with {his} tea.

choices.text: Carry {npc} and the teapot both

mem.note: carried me out to the moon

effects.log: {npc} shrieks and threatens you with the teapot. You sit {him} on the cushioned stool under the moon, and get a dignified kiss on the cheek for your trouble.

events.text: On the same street, facing each other, stand two mooncake shops whose owners have not spoken in twenty years. Before Mid-Autumn, both of them catch you in the street and beg you to say whose mooncakes are better.

choices.text: Taste both and tell the truth

effects.log: One has better crust, the other better filling. You say exactly that. Both owners are furious, and both send you a box.

choices.text: Say both are the best you have ever had

effects.log: Both owners are delighted. Both raise their prices. You have made a terrible mistake.

events.text: Mid-Autumn again, and the feud has worsened. One shop has hung a sign: Better Crust. The other: Better Filling. Children stand in the street reading them aloud.

choices.text: Suggest they make one mooncake together

effects.log: It takes weeks of shuttling between shops. On the festival a single mooncake, crust from one, filling from the other, goes on sale. It sells out in an hour.

choices.text: Buy from both every year, loyally

effects.log: You become the only customer who goes to both. Each owner asks about the other in a careless voice, every time.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, and the street is buzzing: the two mooncake owners have been seen drinking tea together. Now they want you to judge a joint mooncake contest for the whole town.

choices.text: Judge the contest fairly

effects.log: A hundred mooncakes, one stomach. You pick a child's lumpy lotus-seed cake. Both owners agree, which is the first time anyone can remember.

choices.text: Make the two owners judge it with you

effects.log: Three judges arguing about every crumb. The town laughs for weeks. The owners decide the contest should be every year.

events.text: At Mid-Autumn the grown-ups peel a huge pomelo in one piece, and the empty peel goes on a child's head as a hat for luck. It smells wonderful. It covers your eyes.

choices.text: Wear it all evening

effects.log: You walk into the well, the cat and a grandmother. Nobody takes it off you. It is, everyone agrees, extremely lucky.

choices.text: Cut eyeholes in it

effects.log: Now you look like a small, fierce citrus warrior. The other children demand eyeholes too.

events.text: The pomelo hat contest: whoever's hat stays on longest while running round the courtyard wins the last mooncake.

choices.text: Run with your head very still

ok.log: Twelve laps, hat steady, mooncake won. You share it with the smallest child, whose hat fell off on lap one.

fail.log: Your hat flies off into the pond on lap three. A duck wears it briefly. Everyone agrees the duck wins.

choices.text: Tie it on with a ribbon

effects.log: Technically allowed. You win easily. You are also accused of cheating for a year, which you enjoy.

events.text: Mid-Autumn, and a small child of the house holds up a pomelo and a knife and looks at you hopefully.

choices.text: Peel it in one piece

effects.log: It takes a long time and the peel tears twice, but you mend it with a twig. The child wears the hat into the well, the cat and you.

choices.text: Wear the hat yourself, for old times

effects.log: You walk round the courtyard in a pomelo hat, very grave. The child laughs until the hiccups come.

events.arc: Up the Hill Every Double Ninth
events.text: Double Ninth, and everyone climbs high to keep misfortune away. On the hill path you fall in with {npc}, who has climbed this hill every Double Ninth for fifty years and walks it faster than you.

choices.text: Try to keep up

mem.note: tried to keep up with me

effects.log: You arrive at the top gasping. {npc} is already sitting down with a flask of chrysanthemum tea and offers you the cap of it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to set the pace

effects.log: {npc} walks slowly and names every tree. At the top {he} points out the house where {he} was born, which is now a pig farm.

events.arc: Up the Hill Every Double Ninth
events.text: Double Ninth again, the hill, {npc}. This year {he} is slower. Halfway up {he} stops and pretends to admire a rock for quite a long time.

choices.text: Admire the rock with {him}

effects.log: You admire it together for twenty minutes. It is a very ordinary rock. Then you go on at {npc}'s pace and reach the top all the same.

choices.text: Offer your arm

mem.note: gave me an arm up the hill

effects.log: {npc} refuses, then takes it, then makes you carry the tea flask too. 'Since you are offering,' {he} says.

events.arc: Up the Hill Every Double Ninth
events.text: Double Ninth. {npc} cannot climb the hill this year. {He} is sitting at the foot of the path with the tea flask in {his} lap, waiting to hand it to you.

choices.text: Carry {npc} up on your back

effects.log: It takes all morning. At the top {npc} sits on the rock {he} always sat on, very quiet, looking out at the whole province.

choices.text: Climb alone and describe the view on the way down

effects.log: You come back and tell {npc} everything: the river, the pig farm, the far mountains. {He} corrects you on three of the mountains.

events.text: The Double Ninth flower show is all chrysanthemums, and you have grown one in a pot this year: white, lopsided, stubborn. At the show it stands next to a gold one as big as a dinner plate.

choices.text: Show it anyway

effects.log: Your white one wins nothing. An old gardener stops in front of it for a long time and says it has character. You go home happy.

choices.text: Ask the gold one's grower for a secret

effects.log: The grower tells you, eventually, after you admire the gold one at length: pinch the buds, all but one. You go home and pinch.

events.text: Double Ninth, and your chrysanthemum has one bloom on it this year, enormous, the colour of new cream. The gold grower from last year is staring at it.

choices.text: Enter it in the show

effects.log: Second place to the gold one. The gold grower shakes your hand and asks to trade cuttings. This is clearly a great honour.

choices.text: Give it to an old neighbour who cannot climb the hill

effects.log: The neighbour puts it in the window for the festival and says the whole hill came to visit.

events.text: Double Ninth. Your yard is full of chrysanthemums now, white and cream and a gold one from the old rival's cuttings. People walk past just to look.

choices.text: Open the yard for the festival

effects.log: The whole street comes to look, and stays for tea. The gold grower comes too, old now, and sits in the middle and criticises everything fondly.

choices.text: Give a cutting to every child who asks

effects.log: Twenty pots go out of your gate. In ten years the street is the chrysanthemum street.

events.text: On Double Ninth people wear a sprig of dogwood against misfortune. You forgot yours, and halfway up the hill a stranger tucks one behind your ear without a word and walks on.

choices.text: Keep it on all day

effects.log: On the way down, a loose rock crashes onto the path just behind you. You touch the sprig and say thank you to nobody.

choices.text: Run after the stranger to thank them

effects.log: You never catch them. You give your own next year's dogwood to a stranger on the path, without a word, and walk on.

events.text: This year you bring a whole armful of dogwood sprigs up the Double Ninth hill, and tuck them behind the ears of people who forgot theirs.

choices.text: Give them all away
