effects.log: Thirty people walk the hill with your dogwood. A merchant cries. A soldier says thank you very formally. A child steals two.

choices.text: Save the last one for an old woman at the top

effects.log: She has climbed the hill alone with a stick. She takes the sprig, pins it on and tells you that you have a lucky face.

events.text: Double Ninth, and someone tucks a sprig of dogwood behind your ear on the hill path without a word and walks on. You turn, but they are lost in the crowd.

choices.text: Laugh and keep walking

effects.log: So it goes round. You keep the sprig until it is dry, and press it in a book, next to the first one, from years ago.

choices.text: Give it straight to the next person who has none

effects.log: A tired porter, carrying a whole family's food up the hill. The porter looks at you, at the sprig, and laughs out loud.

events.text: Double Ninth is the day for honouring the old. At the street banquet the seat of honour goes to the eldest, a great-grandmother of ninety-four who does not want it and keeps trying to get up and serve.

choices.text: Keep her in her seat, gently

effects.log: Every time she rises you bring her something else she needs. By the end she is laughing and has given up.

choices.text: Let her serve, and carry the plates behind her

effects.log: She serves every table, very slowly, with you carrying everything. It is clearly the best Double Ninth she has had in years.

events.text: Years of Double Ninths. At this year's banquet you are not the youngest at the table any more, nor even in the middle. The young are serving you.

choices.text: Sit and be served, graciously

effects.log: A child brings you tea with both hands, the way you were taught to. You remember being that child, and say thank you properly.

choices.text: Get up and serve anyway

effects.log: Everybody tries to sit you down. You serve every table, very slowly. You understand the old great-grandmother completely now.

events.text: Double Ninth, and the seat of honour at the street banquet is empty, waiting for you. Everyone is watching. You are, it seems, the eldest.

choices.text: Take the seat, and make a short speech

effects.log: You tell them about the great-grandmother who would not stay sitting. Everyone laughs. Then you sit, and stay sitting, mostly.

choices.text: Insist the youngest child sits in it with you

effects.log: The child sits in your lap in the seat of honour and eats all your chrysanthemum cake. It is the right choice.

events.arc: The Tea Seller at the Top
events.text: At the top of the Double Ninth hill {npc} sells chrysanthemum tea from a bucket, and has done so since before anyone can remember. The tea is cold and bitter and costs too much, and everyone buys it.

choices.text: Buy a cup and drink it, wincing (1 tael)

effects.log: It is terrible. {npc} watches you drink every drop and nods, as if you have passed a test.

choices.text: Ask why it is so bitter

effects.log: {npc} says bitter tea at the top of a hill keeps misfortune away. Sweet tea just keeps you on the hill. You decide not to argue.

events.arc: The Tea Seller at the Top
events.text: {npc}'s bucket is at the top of the hill again, but {npc} is sitting beside it with a twisted ankle and cannot ladle. A queue is forming, and nobody knows what to do.

choices.text: Ladle the tea for {npc} all day

effects.log: You serve a thousand cups of bitter tea. {npc} counts the coins and sends half your way, which you refuse, and {he} sends it again.

choices.text: Carry {npc} down to a bonesetter

mem.note: carried me down to the bonesetter

effects.log: The queue groans. {npc} grumbles the whole way down. The bonesetter fixes the ankle and {npc} is back on the hill by afternoon.

events.arc: The Tea Seller at the Top
events.text: Double Ninth. At the top of the hill there is no bucket and no {npc}, only a young person with a bucket of cold, bitter tea, who says {npc} sent them, and that you were to have the first cup free.

choices.text: Drink it, wincing, for {npc}

mem.note: drank my tea to the last

effects.log: It is exactly as bad as ever. You drink every drop. The young one nods at you the way {npc} always did.

choices.text: Go down and visit {npc}

mem.note: came down the hill to see me

effects.log: {npc} is at home with a blanket and a cup of tea, sweet tea, which {he} says is only for invalids and keeps you on the hill.

events.text: Double Ninth cake has nine layers, for the ninth day of the ninth month, and you have been allowed to make it this year. By layer six it is leaning.

choices.text: Prop it with chopsticks

effects.log: Nine layers, four chopsticks, one small flag on top. It looks like a pagoda in a storm. It tastes very good.

choices.text: Eat the leaning layers and start again

effects.log: You eat three layers and make three more. The cake is now perfect, and you are slightly ill.

events.text: The cake again, and this year you are determined to make it straight. You have studied pagodas.

choices.text: Build nine perfect layers

ok.log: Straight as a pine. You put a paper flag on top and carry it out like a treasure. The grown-ups are visibly impressed.

fail.log: Layer eight slides. You catch it in your hands. The cake is now eight layers and a handful. Everyone eats the handful first.

choices.text: Make nine tiny cakes instead

effects.log: Nine little cakes in a tower of plates. It is technically correct and everyone is too charmed to argue.

events.text: Double Ninth, and a child of the house wants to make the cake and will not be helped. By layer six it is leaning.

choices.text: Hand over four chopsticks without a word

effects.log: The child props it, frowning, and puts a flag on top. You say it looks like a pagoda in a storm. The child is very proud.

choices.text: Tell the child about your pagoda in a storm

effects.log: The child laughs so hard the cake falls over. You both eat it off the table.

events.text: On the winter solstice the old ones hang up a paper with a plum branch of eighty-one blank petals: one to fill in each day, nine nines, until spring. This year the paper is given to you.

choices.text: Paint one petal every morning

effects.log: Red petal, red petal, red petal. By the end of winter the whole branch is in bloom on the wall, and outside the real plum is budding.

choices.text: Paint the petals by the weather

effects.log: Red for sun, white for snow, grey for wind. The branch at the end of winter is a record of the whole season. The old ones say nobody has done that in years.

events.text: Solstice again, and a new nine-nines paper. A sick neighbour's child cannot get out of bed this winter and is bored to tears.

choices.text: Give the child the paper to paint

effects.log: The child paints a petal a day. At the eighty-first, the child is walking again, and comes to show you the branch.

choices.text: Paint a second branch for the child to copy yours

effects.log: Two branches bloom across two windows, petal by petal, all winter. You wave to each other every morning.

events.text: The winter solstice, and someone has left a nine-nines paper on your door, already with the first petal painted. The handwriting is a child's.

choices.text: Paint one every morning, all winter

effects.log: You have not done it in years. By the end of winter you have found that you are waiting for each morning, which you had forgotten how to do.

choices.text: Find the child and paint them side by side

effects.log: You and the child paint at the same hour every morning, one at each window. It is the warmest winter in a long time.

events.text: On the longest night a thin child is standing at the gate of the dumpling shop, watching the steam. {npc} says nothing and does not move. The shop is warm. The street is not.

choices.text: Buy {npc} a bowl of dumplings (2 taels)

mem.note: bought me dumplings on the longest night

effects.log: {npc} eats as if the bowl might be taken back. Then {he} says thank you very formally and disappears into the snow.

choices.text: Bring {npc} inside to the stove

mem.note: brought me in from the snow

effects.log: The shopkeeper frowns, then gives {npc} a stool by the stove and a bowl of broth. {npc} falls asleep there, and nobody wakes {him}.

events.text: The longest night again. {npc} is at the dumpling shop gate, but this time {he} is wearing an apron and shouting orders: the shopkeeper took {him} on as a kitchen hand.

choices.text: Order the biggest bowl and tip well (3 taels)

mem.note: came back to my dumpling shop

effects.log: {npc} brings you a bowl piled so high it threatens the ceiling. {He} will not take the tip and you hide it under the bowl.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you to fold the dumplings

effects.log: {npc} is a hard teacher. Yours are lumpy. {He} eats one, makes a face, and says you have potential.

events.text: Solstice night, and the dumpling shop has a new sign with {npc}'s name on it. At the gate stands a thin child watching the steam, and {npc} is already walking out with a bowl.

choices.text: Watch from the street and say nothing

mem.note: saw me do what they did

effects.log: {npc} sits the child by the stove. Then {he} sees you across the street, and nods once. You both know.

choices.text: Go in and eat with them both

mem.note: sat by my stove on the longest night

effects.log: Three bowls by the stove on the longest night. The child asks who you are. {npc} says, the one who started it.

events.text: On the solstice everyone eats tangyuan, sweet rice balls in syrup, and an old custom says you eat one for every year of your age. You are small enough that this is easy. The old ones at the table are suffering.

choices.text: Help an old uncle finish his

effects.log: You eat eleven of his. He thanks you with tears in his eyes and gives you a copper. You are sick, and rich.

choices.text: Count everyone's rice balls out loud

effects.log: You count every bowl in the house, loudly, to the end. The old ones beg you to stop. It is the funniest solstice in years.

events.text: The solstice, and the tangyuan count is no longer easy. You stare at your bowl, which is mostly rice ball.

choices.text: Eat every one, for honour

effects.log: You finish. You cannot stand up. A child comes and helps you finish the syrup, kindly.

choices.text: Count the decades, one rice ball each

effects.log: You eat a ball for every ten years and make a speech about it. The old ones adopt your method at once.

events.text: The longest night, and a child of the house is sitting beside you, counting your rice balls with enormous satisfaction. It will not be possible.

choices.text: Ask the child to help you, the old way

effects.log: The child eats twenty of yours. You give the child a copper. The child is sick and rich, and very happy.

choices.text: Eat one, and tell the child the rest are for the years to come

effects.log: The child thinks about this very seriously, and eats one of your future years for you. It is delicious.

events.arc: Ghost Stories on the Longest Night
events.text: The longest night is the darkest of the year, and the children of the lane gather round a brazier to tell ghost stories. A big girl from the end house tells one about a hand under the bed. Everyone screams.

choices.text: Tell a scarier one

effects.log: Yours is about a ghost who only wants to borrow salt. It is not scary at all, and everyone laughs, and then everyone goes home and checks their salt jar.

choices.text: Walk the smallest child home after

effects.log: The small one holds your hand so tight it hurts. At the door the child whispers that you are very brave. You are not, but you say thank you.

events.arc: Ghost Stories on the Longest Night
events.text: The longest night, the brazier again. This year the big girl from the end house has a story about the empty house at the end of the lane, and dares everyone to knock on its door.

choices.text: Knock on the door

ok.log: The door creaks open. A very old cat looks out, unimpressed, and closes it with its tail. You are a hero in the lane for a year.

fail.log: Nothing happens. Then a pigeon bursts out of the eaves. You run all the way home and blame the wind.

choices.text: Say the empty house is just sad, not haunted

effects.log: Everyone looks at you. Then the big girl says, yes, actually. You go and leave a lantern on its step, all of you together.

events.arc: Ghost Stories on the Longest Night
events.text: On the longest night, the lane's children knock on your door: there is no brazier this year, and they want ghost stories, and somebody says you know the best ones.

choices.text: Tell the salt ghost story

effects.log: They laugh, then go home and check their salt jars. Some things last.

choices.text: Light a brazier and let them tell theirs

effects.log: You sit and listen. One small child tells a story about a hand under the bed, a little different from the one you heard, and everyone screams.

events.text: On the winter solstice an old astronomer from the county observatory measures the noon shadow of a tall bronze gnomon, as has been done for a thousand years. {npc} needs someone to hold the measuring rod still.

choices.text: Hold the rod

effects.log: You hold it so still that {npc} measures the shadow to a hair. {He} writes down the number as if it were a poem.

choices.text: Ask why the shadow matters

effects.log: {npc} explains: the longest shadow of the year tells you the year has turned, and the calendar is right. Then {he} explains for another hour.

events.text: The solstice again, at the gnomon. This year the shadow is wrong by the width of a grain of rice, and {npc} is in despair: either the bronze has moved, or the heavens have.

choices.text: Check the gnomon's footing

mem.note: found the tilt in my gnomon

ok.log: A frost heave has tilted the stone base. You and {npc} jack it level with wedges. The shadow is right again, and the heavens are spared.

mem.note: looked for the fault with me

fail.log: You find nothing wrong. {npc} decides the heavens have moved and writes a long letter to the capital about it.

choices.text: Tell {npc} a grain of rice is not much

mem.note: did not see the grain of rice

effects.log: {npc} looks at you in horror, then laughs. 'A grain a year,' {he} says, 'and in a thousand years the New Year falls in summer.'

events.text: The solstice. {npc} is too frail to climb to the gnomon this year. A young clerk from the observatory asks if you will take the measurement in {npc}'s place, since you know how.

choices.text: Take the measurement and carry it to {npc}

effects.log: You hold the rod, read the shadow to a hair, and run the number to {npc}'s house. {He} writes it in the book in {his} own hand.

choices.text: Teach the young clerk to do it properly

effects.log: You show the clerk how still the rod must be held. The clerk's hands shake. You stand behind and steady them. The shadow is right.

events.arc: Cold Feet on the Longest Night
events.text: The longest night, and the house is freezing. {npc} gets into bed with feet so cold you shout out loud.

choices.text: Warm {npc}'s feet with your hands

mem.note: warmed my feet on the longest night

effects.log: You complain the whole time. {npc} falls asleep smiling. Your hands are frozen.

choices.text: Heat a brick in the stove and wrap it

effects.log: You wrap the hot brick in a cloth and put it at the foot of the bed. {npc} declares it the most romantic thing ever done.

events.arc: Cold Feet on the Longest Night
events.text: Solstice night again. You come to bed and there is already a hot brick wrapped at your feet, and {npc} is pretending to be asleep.

choices.text: Pretend you did not notice

mem.note: laughed in the dark with me

effects.log: You both lie there pretending. It lasts about three breaths before you both laugh.

choices.text: Put your cold feet on {npc} anyway

effects.log: {npc} shrieks. The brick falls out of bed. The neighbours hear everything. It is a very good solstice.

events.arc: Cold Feet on the Longest Night
events.text: The longest night. There are two bricks in the stove now, one each, and a third for the dog's basket, and {npc} wraps them all with the same old cloth.

choices.text: Take over the wrapping this year

effects.log: {npc} supervises from under the quilt, and says you do it wrong, and you do it {his} way.

choices.text: Sit up by the stove together till midnight

mem.note: sat up with me on the longest night

effects.log: Two old people by the stove on the longest night, talking about the first solstice with cold feet. The bricks go cold. Nobody minds.

events.arc: The Firecracker War of Two Streets
events.text: New Year, and the children of your street and the children of the next street have declared war: whoever sets off the loudest firecracker at midnight wins the year. The other street has a cousin who works at a firework shop.

choices.text: Pool everyone's red envelope money

effects.log: Your street buys one enormous firecracker. At midnight it goes off with a sound like the sky splitting. Every dog in town barks for an hour. You win.

choices.text: Propose a truce and one firecracker together

effects.log: Both streets chip in. The firecracker is set off on the corner between them, and both streets claim it was theirs.

events.arc: The Firecracker War of Two Streets
events.text: The firecracker war again, and this time the other street's firecracker has fallen in a puddle, and its children are in despair.

choices.text: Give them half of yours

effects.log: Two streets, two firecrackers, one fuse each, lit together. Nobody wins. Everyone says it was the best New Year.

choices.text: Dry theirs by your stove

effects.log: It dries just in time. It is the loudest bang in the history of the war. The other street wins, because of you, and is very confused about it.

events.arc: The Firecracker War of Two Streets
events.text: New Year's Eve. Two gangs of small children are glaring at each other across the corner of two streets, clutching firecrackers. Someone has told them about the war.

choices.text: Tell them about the truce

effects.log: They listen, scornful, then light their firecrackers together on the corner. You stand back and cover your ears, like an elder.

choices.text: Buy them both a firecracker (2 taels)

effects.log: Two enormous bangs. Both streets win. Both streets will be at war again next year, which is how it should be.

events.text: On Lantern night the old ones float paper lotus lanterns down the river, one for each person they have lost. You have a lotus lantern too, and are not sure whom to send it to.

choices.text: Send it for someone from your own life

effects.log: You think of a face, light the candle and set it on the water. It joins a hundred others going round the bend.

choices.text: Send it for somebody nobody remembers

effects.log: You send it for whoever has no lantern. An old fisherman beside you nods and does the same with his last one.

events.text: Lantern night by the river again. A small child beside you is crying: the child's lotus lantern has tipped over and gone out.

choices.text: Light yours and give it to the child

effects.log: The child sets it on the water very carefully and watches it all the way round the bend. You go home without one, which is fine.

choices.text: Show the child how to fold a new one

effects.log: You fold a lotus from a page of your own notebook. It is ugly. It floats. The child is beside the water until it is gone.

events.text: On Lantern night someone has set a lotus lantern on your doorstep, already folded, with a note: for whoever you are sending it to. The handwriting is a child's.

choices.text: Float it on the river

effects.log: It goes round the bend with the others. You stand there for a long time after.

choices.text: Fold a second one and leave it on another step

effects.log: You leave it with a note in your own hand. Somebody else's doorstep, somebody else's lantern night.

events.text: At Qingming the household always leaves plums on the grave of a great-great-grandparent who, the story goes, loved plums above everything. Every year the plums are gone by morning. The old ones say the ancestor eats them.

choices.text: Hide behind a tomb and watch

effects.log: At dusk a monkey comes down from the hill, takes the plums one by one and eats them on the tombstone, very politely. You decide not to tell anyone.

choices.text: Leave an extra plum, for manners

effects.log: The next morning there is a plum stone left neatly on the grave, like a thank you. You are almost sure that is a good sign.

events.text: Qingming, and you know about the monkey. This year it has brought a baby monkey with it, and the two of them are waiting on the tombstone before you have even set the plums down.

choices.text: Give them the plums, and bow

effects.log: You bow to the monkeys, as to an ancestor. They eat with great dignity. The old ones watch from the path and say the ancestor is pleased.

choices.text: Tell the grown-ups the truth

effects.log: The grown-ups go quiet, then laugh, then decide that a plum-loving ancestor would certainly come back as a monkey. Nothing changes, except the jokes.

events.text: Qingming. You are the one carrying the plums now, and a child of the house is asking why the plums always vanish.

choices.text: Say the ancestor eats them

effects.log: The child is very impressed. At dusk you both hide behind a tomb, and the monkeys come.

choices.text: Bring twice as many plums this year

effects.log: The monkeys leave a pile of stones on the grave, neatly, like a tally. The child counts them all the way home.

events.text: The town has built a new dragon boat, and before it can race the eyes must be dotted with red ink, to wake it. The elders cannot agree who should hold the brush. In the end, out of spite, they choose you.

choices.text: Dot the eyes with a steady hand

ok.log: Two perfect red dots. The dragon wakes; everyone says so. That year the boat wins its first race.

fail.log: The left eye is a little higher than the right. The dragon looks surprised all season. It still wins once.

choices.text: Hand the brush to the oldest rower

effects.log: The oldest rower weeps, dots the eyes, and rows like a young person all festival. The elders, briefly, agree on something.

events.text: The dragon boat's eyes have faded over the winter, and the elders say the one who woke it must wake it again. The brush is waiting for you at the jetty.

choices.text: Dot them again, carefully

effects.log: You redo them exactly. The boat is the same dragon, awake again. It is a good feeling to wake the same thing twice.

choices.text: Let a child dot them with your hand on the brush

effects.log: The child's dots are a little wild. The dragon looks fierce this year. The child tells everyone.

events.text: The old dragon boat is retiring, too old to race, and will hang in the temple hall. Before it goes, the elders want the eyes closed with a stroke of black ink, so it can sleep. They hand you the brush.

choices.text: Close the eyes gently

effects.log: Two strokes of black. The town goes quiet. Then the rowers carry the old boat to the temple on their shoulders, singing.

choices.text: Leave one eye open, to watch the new boat race

effects.log: The elders mutter, then agree. The old dragon hangs in the temple with one eye open, watching the river.

events.text: Qixi in the courtyard, and the women and men of the street are carving melons into flowers, lanterns and fish for the Weaver Girl, to show the skill of their hands. Anyone may enter. A melon is waiting for you.

choices.text: Carve a lotus

ok.log: Your lotus opens petal by petal. The neighbours stop to look. A grandmother carves you a fish in return, as a compliment.

fail.log: Your lotus becomes a cabbage. Then a slightly smaller cabbage. You eat it, which the rules allow.

choices.text: Carve a portrait of the judge

effects.log: It looks like a melon with eyes. The judge laughs so much the contest has to stop. You win a prize for courage.

events.text: The melon carving again. This year a newcomer to the street, a shy young carpenter, has carved a melon into a whole little pavilion, and is too shy to show it.

choices.text: Carry the pavilion to the judges

effects.log: The judges gasp. The carpenter wins and goes red to the ears and has three orders for furniture by morning.

choices.text: Enter your own and lose gladly

effects.log: You enter a modest fish. The pavilion wins. You lead the applause, and the carpenter carves you a tiny melon fish to keep.

events.text: At Qixi the street's children are trying to carve melons and making a great mess, and they look at you, because you carved the cabbage-lotus everyone still talks about.

choices.text: Teach them the lotus

effects.log: Petal, petal, petal. Nine lotuses, mostly cabbages, one real. The children eat their mistakes happily.

choices.text: Carve a cabbage on purpose, for them

effects.log: The children shriek. The cabbage wins the children's prize. You are very proud.

events.text: Before Mid-Autumn the osmanthus tree next door blooms, and the whole lane smells of apricots and honey. The old neighbour who owns it wants help shaking the blossoms down onto a sheet, for osmanthus cakes.

choices.text: Shake the branches

effects.log: Blossom falls like golden snow on you, the sheet and the neighbour's cat. The neighbour makes cakes and sends you a whole plate.

choices.text: Pick them one by one, carefully

effects.log: It takes all day, and the blossoms are perfect. The neighbour says you have patient hands and sends you a jar of osmanthus syrup.

events.text: The osmanthus is blooming again. The old neighbour is unwell this year and cannot make the cakes, and is sitting by the window looking at the tree.

choices.text: Make the cakes yourself from the neighbour's recipe

effects.log: The neighbour directs from the window. The cakes are lumpy. The neighbour eats three and pronounces them correct.

choices.text: Bring a branch to the window

effects.log: You cut one small branch and put it in a jar by the bed. The room smells of apricots and honey for a week. The neighbour sleeps well.

events.text: The old neighbour's house has new people in it now. At Mid-Autumn the osmanthus blooms, and the new people stand under it, puzzled, not knowing what to do with it.

choices.text: Show them how to make the cakes

effects.log: You shake the branches, spread the sheet, and make the cakes in their kitchen. They will make them next year. The tree is in good hands.

choices.text: Plant a cutting in your own yard

effects.log: The new people give you a cutting. In a few years your own yard smells of apricots and honey every autumn.

events.arc: The Old Soldiers on the Hill
events.text: On Double Ninth a group of old soldiers climb to the top of the hill and drink chrysanthemum tea in silence for the ones who did not come home. {npc}, the youngest of them, which is not very young, asks you to carry the tea.

choices.text: Carry the tea and keep quiet

mem.note: carried our tea up the hill

effects.log: You carry the tea and sit apart. At the top they pour a cup for every empty place. {npc} pours one for you too.

choices.text: Ask {npc} about the ones who did not come back

effects.log: {npc} tells you three names, slowly. On the way down {he} tells you two more.

events.arc: The Old Soldiers on the Hill
events.text: Double Ninth, and fewer old soldiers climb the hill this year. {npc} is still there, and asks you to carry the tea again, and to pour.

choices.text: Pour for every empty place

effects.log: There are more empty places than full ones now. You pour every cup. Nobody speaks, and it is the right silence.

choices.text: Bring the youngest of your street to carry it with you

mem.note: brought a child to the hill

effects.log: The child carries the cups and listens to everything. {npc} tells the child the names.

events.arc: The Old Soldiers on the Hill
events.text: Double Ninth. Only {npc} climbs the hill now, slowly, on your arm, with the tea.

choices.text: Pour for all of them, and for {npc}

mem.note: climbed the hill with me last

effects.log: {npc} drinks and names every one. When {he} is done, {he} names one more: {his} own. 'For later,' {he} says. 'You will pour it.'

choices.text: Carry {npc} the last stretch

effects.log: At the top {npc} sits among the empty places and pours the tea unaided, very steadily, one cup at a time.

events.text: On the solstice the river freezes thick, and {npc}, a neighbour with a hand drill and too much optimism, invites you to fish through the ice on the longest night.

choices.text: Go and fish all night

effects.log: You catch two fish and lose all feeling in your feet. {npc} catches nothing and is happier than you. You cook the fish on the ice.

choices.text: Bring a brazier and stay warm

effects.log: You sit by the brazier on the ice, warm and slightly worried about the ice. {npc} fishes. Nobody catches anything, and it is very peaceful.

events.text: The longest night, the ice, {npc} with the drill. This year {npc} has built a little straw hut on the ice with a hole in the floor. It is luxurious.

choices.text: Fish from the hut

effects.log: Warm and dry, you catch a carp as long as your arm. {npc} says the hut was {his} best idea in years and you agree.

choices.text: Help {npc} build a second hut for the neighbours

effects.log: Two huts on the ice. By midnight the whole street is out there, fishing, eating and singing on the river.

events.text: Solstice. {npc} is too old for the ice now, but has drilled the hole anyway, from the bank, with a long pole, and is waiting for you to fish it.

choices.text: Fish the hole and bring {npc} the catch

effects.log: One small fish, cooked on the brazier and shared on the bank. {npc} says it is the best fish of the year, and it is.

choices.text: Carry {npc} out to the old hut

effects.log: You carry {npc} out to the straw hut on the ice. {npc} fishes all night with a blanket on {his} knees, and catches nothing, and is perfectly happy.
